section_summary: This section consists chiefly of letters from clergy, lawyers, educators, church congregations, peace advocates, and other citizens urging the Roosevelt administration to stop American exports of aircraft, oil, scrap iron, cotton, munitions, and credit that supported Japan’s war in China. State Department replies repeatedly explain that the Neutrality Act could not be invoked without a presidential finding of war, did not cover most raw materials, and was not considered prudent to invoke, while emphasizing official condemnation of bombing civilians. The section also addresses the Nine-Power Treaty, aid to belligerents in Spain, petitions and resolutions for nonparticipation or embargoes, eyewitness descriptions of the bombing of Guangzhou, and statistics on licensed arms exports to China and Japan.

subfiles.title: J. S. Burgess to Cordell Hull concerning American supplies to Japan
subfiles.from: J. S. Burgess, Chairman, Department of Sociology, Temple University
subfiles.about: Burgess asks whether exports to Japan can be limited without drawing the United States into war.
subfiles.summary: J. S. Burgess says American oil, cotton, scrap and munitions help Japan destroy China, cites "Japan's Partner," proposes quotas at prewar trade levels, and copies Senators Guffey and Davis.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to J. S. Burgess
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains the legal and policy limits on restricting exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green tells Burgess the Neutrality Act bars arms to China and Japan only after a presidential war finding, doesn't cover oil, cotton or scrap, and the President judged invocation contrary to U.S. interests; license totals and Hull's bombing condemnation included.

subfiles.title: S. Warren Sturgis to the Department of State
subfiles.from: S. Warren Sturgis
subfiles.about: Sturgis urges immediate executive action against American exports supporting Japan’s war.
subfiles.summary: Sturgis deplores the inconsistency of condemning Japanese brutality while supplying Japan with war materials. He asks whether the President or State Department can curtail oil and scrap-iron exports without waiting for Congress to reconvene.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles memorandum to Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles
subfiles.about: Welles requests a draft reply to his former Groton School teacher, S. Warren Sturgis.
subfiles.summary: Welles says Sturgis was a former teacher and asks Hornbeck to draft a personal reply for his signature explaining the government's position and facts.

subfiles.title: Sumner Welles reply to S. Warren Sturgis
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles
subfiles.about: Welles explains the administration’s position on restricting exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The badly reproduced draft gives Sturgis the same Neutrality Act explanation used in other departmental replies. It states that the President has not invoked the act in the Far Eastern conflict and closes with Welles’s personal regards, enclosing the Joint Resolution and the pamphlet International Traffic in Arms.

subfiles.title: Blank or illegible separator page
subfiles.about: The page contains no intelligible substantive document text.
subfiles.summary: Only stray OCR characters and page artifacts appear. It is apparently a blank verso or separator between correspondence units.

subfiles.title: Earl H. Leaf to Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.from: Earl H. Leaf
subfiles.about: Leaf thanks Hornbeck for receiving a committee and reports growing public and religious opposition to aiding Japan.
subfiles.summary: Earl Leaf thinks the committee's Washington visit succeeded, welcomes Senator Pittman's resolution and church support, expects heavy public demands to end U.S. partnership in China's destruction, and attacks Frederick Libby as pro-Japanese.

subfiles.title: Stanley K. Hornbeck reply to Earl H. Leaf
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges Leaf’s letter and thanks him for the information supplied.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck expresses appreciation for Leaf’s courtesy and information. The brief reply offers no substantive comment on Leaf’s political observations.

subfiles.title: Ralph O. Wells to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: Ralph O. Wells
subfiles.about: Wells argues that the Nine-Power Treaty may justify prohibiting gasoline and military supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ralph Wells welcomes Hull's efforts against airplane sales to Japan but asks why gasoline and other supplies can't also be barred, citing the treaty obligation to respect China's integrity.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Ralph O. Wells
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department rejects the contention that the Nine-Power Treaty authorizes an export prohibition.
subfiles.summary: Green tells Wells the Neutrality Act applies to both countries only after a proclamation and doesn't cover non-arms commodities, the Nine-Power Treaty gives no power to prohibit exports, and license totals are given.

subfiles.title: Archie L. Hirst to Franklin D. Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Archie L. Hirst
subfiles.about: Hirst forwards a unanimously adopted Methodist resolution opposing material and financial aid to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Archie Hirst reports about 500 Methodists heard Ralph Diffendorfer on the Sino-Japanese conflict in Madison and asks Roosevelt to help achieve the enclosed resolution's aim.

subfiles.title: Methodist resolution against aid to Japan
subfiles.from: Clergy and laypeople representing forty churches of the West Wisconsin Conference
subfiles.to: President and Congress of the United States
subfiles.about: The resolution endorses a southern Methodist appeal to prevent American resources from aiding Japan’s aggression.
subfiles.summary: Madison Methodists approve the Birmingham resolution urging the President and Congress to stop government or private resources aiding Japan's war on China.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Archie L. Hirst
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department responds to the Methodist resolution by outlining the Neutrality Act and export-license policy.
subfiles.summary: Green tells Hirst arms exports could be barred only after a presidential war finding, non-arms goods are outside the resolution, the President judged invocation not in U.S. interests; license figures included.

subfiles.title: E. Eldredge Brewster to the Secretary of State
subfiles.from: E. Eldredge Brewster
subfiles.about: Brewster asks for an embargo on essential war materials used by aggressors in China and Spain.
subfiles.summary: E. Eldredge Brewster says his congregation fears scrap and oil make the U.S. a participant in Japan's aggression, that missionaries found American-made material in bomb fragments, and seeks assurance of action on bombing in China and Spain.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to E. Eldredge Brewster
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department contrasts the existing Spanish arms embargo with the absence of legal authority for one against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green tells Brewster the Neutrality Act covers declared or serious civil war, Spain alone was under an arms embargo, no finding was made for China and Japan, and oil and scrap are not covered; he quotes Hull's bombing condemnation.

subfiles.title: Gerald Watkins to Franklin D. Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Gerald Watkins
subfiles.about: Watkins asks Roosevelt to stop American war-material shipments that make the United States Japan’s partner.
subfiles.summary: Gerald Watkins cites "Japan's Partner," argues American supplies make Japan's undeclared war possible, calls the policy inconsistent with naval expansion, and urges drastic neutrality enforcement.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Gerald Watkins
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains why the administration has not prohibited supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green tells Watkins the Neutrality Act needs a presidential war finding and would embargo arms to both countries, non-arms goods can't be prohibited, and the President judged invocation contrary to U.S. interests.

subfiles.title: Mrs. F. A. Stromsten to the Secretary of State
subfiles.from: Mrs. F. A. Stromsten
subfiles.about: Stromsten protests the sale of American war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Although much of the handwriting is poorly legible, Stromsten argues that arms and materials manufacturers profit at the expense of Chinese lives. She asks the Department to act and requests a response explaining the government’s position.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Mrs. F. A. Stromsten
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department answers Stromsten’s protest with its standard explanation of neutrality law and policy.
subfiles.summary: Green states that only a presidential war proclamation could activate a bilateral arms embargo and that the President had decided not to invoke the Joint Resolution. He supplies licensed-export values for China and Japan. The reply also repeats Hull’s public condemnation of civilian bombing and its material encouragement.

subfiles.title: Rosa Lee Cosby transmittal letter
subfiles.from: Rosa Lee Cosby, Washington Friends of Spanish Democracy
subfiles.about: Cosby forwards an Executive Committee resolution concerning aircraft and war-material exports.
subfiles.summary: Rosa Lee Cosby sends Hull a resolution of the Washington Friends of Spanish Democracy Executive Committee; letterhead lists officers and sponsors.

subfiles.title: Washington Friends of Spanish Democracy resolution
subfiles.from: Executive Committee, Washington Friends of Spanish Democracy
subfiles.about: The resolution urges Hull to discourage and refuse licenses for exports aiding attacks on civilians in China and Spain.
subfiles.summary: Committee commends Hull for discouraging aircraft sales to Japan and calls for the same policy on planes, oil and scrap to Italy and Germany for attacks on the Spanish Republic.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Rosa Lee Cosby
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains that no presidential war finding supports an arms embargo against Japan, Italy, or Germany.
subfiles.summary: Green tells Cosby the Neutrality Act requires an arms ban only after a presidential war finding, none exists for Japan, Italy or Germany, so State has no authority, and non-arms goods are outside it.

subfiles.title: Paul G. Hayes to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: Paul G. Hayes
subfiles.about: Hayes asks for lawful executive action to end American participation in Japan’s aggression.
subfiles.summary: Paul Hayes praises efforts against bombing-plane exports, argues Japan depends on American supplies, and asks whether any law could support a comprehensive embargo without war, as nonparticipation.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Paul G. Hayes
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department describes the statutory limits and policy reasons against an embargo on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green tells Hayes an arms embargo needs a presidential war finding and would apply to both countries, non-arms goods can't be prohibited, invocation wouldn't serve U.S. interests; license totals provided.

subfiles.title: G. Ashton Oldham to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: G. Ashton Oldham, Bishop of Albany
subfiles.about: Oldham forwards Fred H. Lysons’s legal argument for ending arms traffic with Japan.
subfiles.summary: G. Ashton Oldham hopes a way is found to stop the arms traffic, believes most Americans want that, and encloses Lysons's letter.

subfiles.title: Fred H. Lysons to G. Ashton Oldham
subfiles.from: Fred H. Lysons
subfiles.about: Lysons argues that treaty enforcement, rather than a neutrality embargo, can halt American supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Fred Lysons contends furnishing Japan supplies makes the U.S. a participant in the assault on China and violates the Nine-Power Treaty, proposes Roosevelt suspend shipments pending review, and urges organized public pressure.

subfiles.title: R. Walton Moore reply to G. Ashton Oldham
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, Counselor
subfiles.about: Moore rejects Lysons’s interpretation of the Nine-Power Treaty and reiterates neutrality policy.
subfiles.summary: Moore tells Oldham the Nine-Power Treaty gives no authority to prohibit exports, a Neutrality Act embargo needs a war finding and applies to both sides; license figures given, Lysons's letter returned.

subfiles.title: W. Russell Bowie to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: W. Russell Bowie, Rector of Grace Church
subfiles.about: Bowie cites aircraft and aviation-fuel exports and asks how the United States can stop being Japan’s accomplice.
subfiles.summary: W. Russell Bowie quotes a Foreign Policy Association bulletin on American aviation fuel and aircraft sales making the U.S. a silent partner in Japanese aggression, and asks for action.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to W. Russell Bowie
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: The Department outlines the Neutrality Act and Hull’s position on bombing aircraft.
subfiles.summary: Green tells Bowie a war finding would embargo both China and Japan, goods outside the arms list can't be restricted, the President judged invocation contrary to U.S. interests; license totals and Hull's bombing condemnation included.

subfiles.title: Paul G. Hayes covering letter forwarding a Calvary Methodist resolution
subfiles.from: Paul G. Hayes
subfiles.about: Hayes forwards a petition calling for a policy of nonparticipation in Japanese aggression.
subfiles.summary: Hayes acknowledges Green's June 30 explanation and concedes the President lacks authority, asks for a nonparticipation policy and legislation, and argues a materials and credit embargo would pressure Japan without provoking war.

subfiles.title: Calvary Methodist petition to Franklin D. Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Members of Calvary Methodist Episcopal Church, Minneapolis
subfiles.about: The petition asks Roosevelt to use every lawful means to prevent American material and financial assistance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Calvary Methodist petition names Japan aggressor, condemns attacks on Chinese cities and hospitals, alleges American materials, aircraft and credits sustain it, and asks government to prevent direct or indirect aid.

subfiles.title: Signatures to the Calvary Methodist petition
subfiles.from: Members of Calvary Methodist Episcopal Church
subfiles.about: The sheet records the names and addresses of the people signing the July 3 petition.
subfiles.summary: About forty signers of the Calvary Methodist petition with Minneapolis-area addresses; Paul Hayes certifies the copy.

subfiles.title: Department of State acknowledgment to Paul G. Hayes
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges receipt of the Calvary Methodist resolution.
subfiles.summary: Green summarizes the resolution against American aid to Japan, thanks Hayes and promises careful attention without a further policy explanation.

subfiles.title: Mary E. Woolley to the Secretary of State
subfiles.from: Mary E. Woolley
subfiles.about: Woolley proposes publicly identifying firms that export important war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Mary Woolley, citing confidential reports from Nanjing and Guangzhou, asks whether publishing the names of firms exporting scrap, oil and cotton might succeed where humanitarian appeals failed.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull reply to Mary E. Woolley
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges Woolley’s proposal but says further action is not presently feasible.
subfiles.summary: Hull promises full consideration, encloses the Joint Resolution and arms-traffic pamphlet, explains scrap, oil and cotton aren't covered by the arms proclamation, and declines to go further now.

subfiles.title: Stuart Innerst to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: Stuart Innerst, First United Brethren Church
subfiles.about: Innerst forwards a Guangzhou appeal and asks why neutrality law has not stopped war-supply shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Stuart Innerst read the Canton Committee letter to about two hundred people, who voted unanimously to send it to Hull; he asks why the neutrality law hasn't produced action.

subfiles.title: Canton Committee for Justice to China appeal
subfiles.from: A. D. Fisher and Edward H. Lockwood, Canton Committee for Justice to China
subfiles.about: The committee describes Japanese bombing casualties in Guangzhou and calls for organized pressure on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Canton Committee for Justice to China circular describes bombing of Guangzhou and its casualties, asks communities to consider a boycott, defensive aid and relief, and argues helping China could avert a later war.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Stuart Innerst
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: The Department explains why neutrality legislation has not stopped exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green tells Innerst no authority exists to embargo arms to Japan alone or both countries without a war finding, defends not invoking the act, gives revised license totals and repeats Hull's bombing condemnation.

subfiles.title: Jessie O. Butts to the Secretary of State
subfiles.from: Jessie O. Butts
subfiles.about: Butts asks whether the President can embargo aircraft and other war materials going to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The first page is partly duplicated or fragmentary, but the letter clearly protests the sale of bombing planes and other military materials to Japan. Butts asks about Roosevelt’s legal power to impose an embargo and calls American opposition to bombing hypocritical while the country supplies material used against defenseless civilians.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Jessie O. Butts
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Chief, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: The Department answers Butts’s embargo question with its standard interpretation of neutrality law.
subfiles.summary: Green tells Jessie Butts only a presidential war finding could trigger a Neutrality Act embargo, covering both China and Japan, the President declined to invoke it, and cites Hull's civilian-bombing condemnation; license figures given.

subfiles.title: Henry Stauffer to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: Henry Stauffer
subfiles.about: Stauffer criticizes nominal neutrality that in practice favors Japan and forwards material concerning T. Z. Koo.
subfiles.summary: Henry Stauffer, in a partly degraded letter, argues U.S. policy is effectively pro-Japanese despite condemnation; his enclosed church bulletin records T. Z. Koo's address on China.

subfiles.title: First Congregational Church bulletin featuring T. Z. Koo
subfiles.from: First Congregational Church, Berkeley
subfiles.about: The bulletin announces worship services and an evening address by T. Z. Koo entitled “What of China?”
subfiles.summary: First Congregational Church bulletin: worship and a sermon by Oswald McCall, with an evening address by T. Z. Koo under the Institute of International Relations at Mills College, plus staff and notices.
